text: An ice age is a long stretch of time when Earth has big sheets of ice on land, far from the mountains. Earth has had several. The most recent one began about 2.6 million years ago and, strictly speaking, hasn't ended, because Antarctica and Greenland are still covered in ice.

Within this long ice age, the planet has swung back and forth between cold glacial periods, when [[@what-if-ice-melted|ice sheets]] spread, and warmer interglacials, when they shrink. We live in a warm interglacial that began about 11,700 years ago. When people talk about "the Ice Age", they usually mean the last cold spell, which peaked about 20,000 years ago.

st.reveal: So much water was locked up in ice sheets on land that the sea dropped by about 120 m. Land bridges appeared, joining Asia to Alaska, Britain to Europe, and India to Sri Lanka.

sec.t:
At the height of the last glacial period, a sheet of ice more than 3 km thick sat over Hudson Bay in Canada. It spread south over the places where Chicago and New York now stand. Another ice sheet covered Scandinavia and much of Britain.

[[glacier|Glaciers]] in the Himalaya grew longer and reached lower [[@valleys|valleys]]. Average temperatures around the world were several degrees colder than today. Many places were also drier, because cold air holds less moisture. The [[@thar-formed|Thar Desert]] spread, and [[@monsoon|the monsoon]] was weaker.

All that ice was water taken from the ocean. As the ice sheets grew, the sea fell by about 120 metres, roughly the height of a 40-storey building.

New land appeared. A wide plain called Beringia joined Siberia to [[@alaska|Alaska]], and people and animals crossed it into the Americas. Britain was joined to Europe. A ridge of land linked southern India to [[@sri-lanka|Sri Lanka]] in the shallow sea where the chain of islands and sandbanks called Adam's Bridge, or Ram Setu, lies today.

sec.h: Why the ice comes and goes
sec.t:
In the 1830s, the Swiss-American scientist Louis Agassiz argued that giant boulders scattered across Europe had been carried by ice. Many scientists doubted him at first. Today the evidence is overwhelming.

But why does the ice advance and retreat? In the early 1900s, the Serbian scientist Milutin Milanković worked out that small, regular changes in Earth's [[orbit|orbit]] and tilt change how much summer sunlight reaches the far north. These cycles repeat roughly every 23,000, 41,000 and 100,000 years. When northern summers are cool, snow doesn't melt, and ice sheets grow.

Changes in the air add to the effect. In cold periods, the air held less [[carbon-dioxide|carbon dioxide]], a gas that traps heat. Bubbles of ancient air trapped in Antarctic ice show this clearly.

Much further back, about 700 million years ago, Earth may have gone through even harsher ice ages. Some scientists think ice reached almost to the [[equator|equator]], an idea called Snowball Earth. Others think a band of open water stayed near the equator. This is still being argued over.

Without people, Earth would probably stay in this warm interglacial for tens of thousands of years. But burning coal, oil and gas has pushed carbon dioxide higher than it has been for hundreds of thousands of years. Today's [[@climate-change|warming]] is happening much faster than the natural swings of the Ice Ages.

text: There are eight planets, and their order going out from the Sun is Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune. The easiest way to remember them is a mnemonic, a silly sentence where each word starts with the same letter as a planet.

The most famous is "My Very Educated Mother Just Served Us Noodles". Some people say Nachos instead. If you prefer your own, you can make one up: "Many Volcanoes Erupt Mightily, Jumping Super Unusual Nights" works just as well. The sillier the sentence, the better your [[@memory|memory]] tends to hold on to it.

options.t: Venus, the second planet

st.reveal: Venus is wrapped in a thick blanket of carbon dioxide that traps heat, so its surface is around 465°C, hot enough to melt lead. Mercury has almost no air, so its night side gets very cold. Being closest to the Sun is not the whole story.

sec.t:
Older books had a sentence with nine words, like "My Very Excellent Mother Just Served Us Nine Pizzas". The P stood for [[@pluto|Pluto]]. In 2006, the International Astronomical Union decided that Pluto did not meet its new definition of a planet, because it hasn't cleared its path of other objects. Pluto became a dwarf planet.

So the mother stopped serving pizzas. Many children were upset, and some scientists still argue about the decision. Out past Neptune, there are many more small icy worlds, and several are called [[@dwarf-planets|dwarf planets]] too.

sec.h: Planets in Hindi and your week
sec.t:
In Hindi, the planets have names that many children already know from the days of the week: Budh (Mercury), Shukra (Venus), Mangal (Mars), Brihaspati or Guru (Jupiter) and Shani (Saturn). So Mangalvar, Tuesday, is the day of Mars, and Shanivar, Saturday, is the day of Saturn. English does the same thing with Saturday.

Uranus and Neptune can't be seen without a telescope and were only discovered in 1781 and 1846. In Hindi they are often called Arun and Varun. Ancient [[@astronomy-ancient-india|Indian astronomers]], like those in many other cultures, tracked only the planets they could see with their own eyes.

Diagrams usually show the planets spaced neatly, but real distances are huge and uneven. If the Sun were a football at one end of a cricket ground, Earth would be a peppercorn about 25 metres away. Jupiter would be a large marble about 125 metres away. Neptune would be a small bead about 750 metres off, far outside the stadium.

Neptune is about 30 times farther from the Sun than Earth. Light from the Sun takes about eight minutes to reach us, but about four hours to reach Neptune. A year on Neptune lasts about 165 Earth years, so it has gone round the Sun only about once since it was discovered.

sec.h: Which planet is closest to Earth?
sec.t:
Most people say Venus, because Venus comes closer to us than any other planet. But in 2019, a small group of researchers worked out the average distance over many years. Venus spends long stretches on the far side of the Sun.

Mercury, circling tightly near the Sun, never gets very far from anyone. On average, it is the closest planet to Earth, and to every other planet too. Order in space depends on what question you ask.

text: Birds sing mostly to say two things: "this patch is mine" and "choose me". In the breeding season, a male's song warns other males away from his [[territory|territory]] and attracts a mate. The dawn chorus is the burst of song that starts just before sunrise.

Why dawn? Scientists have several ideas. The air is often still and cool at daybreak, so sound carries farther. It is too dark to hunt insects well, so [[@singing|singing]] wastes little feeding time. And a loud song at first light shows neighbours that the singer has survived the night and is still in charge. Each idea has some evidence, and the answer may differ from [[species|species]] to species.

st.prompt: Why do you think birds sing at dawn?

options.t: Sound carries far in calm morning air
Too dark to find food yet
To say ‘this is my place!’

st.reveal: All three might be true! Scientists have several ideas. Morning air is still and cool, so songs travel farther. It's too dark to hunt insects, so it's a good time to sing. And songs tell neighbours ‘this is my territory’ and attract mates.

quiz.prompt: Where does a songbird's song come from?

options.t: An organ deep in its chest where the windpipe splits in two
Vocal cords in its throat, just like ours
Clicking the two halves of its beak together

quiz.reveal: Birds sing with a syrinx, which sits where the windpipe divides into two tubes for the lungs. Each side can work on its own, so some birds can sing two different notes at the same time.

Ali S. & Ripley S.D. Handbook of the Birds of India and Pakistan (Asian koel).
n.certNote: Birds clearly sing to defend territory and attract mates. Why so much of it happens at dawn has several competing explanations, and different ones may fit different species.

sec.h: A voice box in the chest
sec.t:
You make sounds with [[@voice|vocal cords]] in your throat. Birds have something quite different: a [[syrinx|syrinx]] (say "SIR-inks"), deep in the chest where the windpipe splits in two. Air rushing out of the [[@lungs-breathe|lungs]] makes thin walls inside it vibrate.

Because the two sides of the syrinx can work separately, some birds sing two notes at once and seem to harmonise with themselves. Birds' songs are fast. Some notes come too quickly for our ears to separate, though slowing a recording reveals them, a bit like slowing down [[@music-notes|written music]] to see each note.

Birdwatchers often find birds by ear long before they see them. Phone apps can now listen to a recording and suggest which birds are singing. Each February, people around the world, including thousands in India, join the Great Backyard Bird Count, which began in North America in 1998. They count birds for at least 15 minutes and share their lists, helping scientists see how bird numbers change.

Recordings show that the dawn chorus itself is changing. In 2021, scientists rebuilt the sound of thousands of spring mornings in Europe and North America over 25 years. They found the chorus had become quieter and less varied in many places, as many common birds grew rarer. A loud, busy morning chorus is a sign of a place where plenty of birds still live.

In much of India, summer has a soundtrack: the koel's rising "ku-oo, ku-oo", often before dawn. That loud singer is a male. The female, speckled brown, has a sharper call.

Koels do not build nests. A female lays her eggs in the nest of a crow, often while her mate distracts the crow owners. The crows then raise the koel chick as their own. This kind of trick is called brood parasitism. It is risky, because [[@crow-smart|crows are clever]] and sometimes spot the intruder. In [[@urban-wildlife|noisy cities]], some birds have changed too. Studies in Britain found robins singing at night where daytime traffic noise was loudest.

text: The lion-tailed macaque is a monkey found only in the rainforests of the Western Ghats, in Kerala, Tamil Nadu and Karnataka. It has glossy black fur and a thick silver-white mane framing its face, like a grey beard. Its tail ends in a little tuft, a bit like a lion's, which gives it its name.

It is one of the rarest monkeys in India. Only a few thousand live in the wild, by most estimates, and the IUCN lists it as Endangered. The main threat is the loss and breaking up of its forest by tea and coffee estates, roads and dams.

st.prompt: Where do lion-tailed macaques spend most of their time?

On open grassland
In caves

st.reveal: Lion-tailed macaques are tree-dwellers. They feed, travel and sleep high in the canopy of evergreen rainforests and rarely come down to the ground. That is why cutting forests into pieces, with roads and plantations in between, hurts them so much.

sec.h: The monkey that saved a forest
sec.t:
In the 1970s, the Kerala government planned a [[hydroelectric|hydroelectric]] dam in Silent Valley, a stretch of rainforest so quiet that it seemed to have no cicadas. Scientists, writers, poets and local people objected. They argued that the dam would flood one of India's last untouched [[@rainforests|rainforests]] and the home of the lion-tailed macaque.

The macaque became the face of the campaign, appearing on posters and in newspapers. In 1983 the dam plan was dropped, and in 1984 Silent Valley became a national park. It is often remembered as one of India's first big environmental victories, alongside movements like Chipko, and part of the story of [[@environment-heroes|environment heroes]].

Many lion-tailed macaques today live in small forest patches surrounded by tea and coffee estates. One famous area is the Valparai plateau in the Anamalai Hills of Tamil Nadu, where troops survive in fragments of rainforest.

The problem is roads. To reach other patches, the monkeys must come down and cross busy roads, where some are hit by vehicles. Researchers estimated that at least 40 macaques died on Valparai's roads over about two years, mostly in accidents.

Conservationists came up with a clever answer: canopy bridges, ropes or nets strung between trees on either side of the road, so monkeys can cross above the traffic. In 2025 and 2026, the Tamil Nadu forest department put up 10 canopy bridges in the Valparai and Manombolly ranges, and the macaques began using them.

Forest officials also put up speed breakers and signboards, and volunteers stand by roads to slow traffic when troops cross. Planting native trees between forest patches helps reconnect the canopy for the future. Some tea estates now leave strips of forest standing along streams, giving the monkeys safe corridors.

The [[@western-ghats|Western Ghats]] are older than the Himalayas and full of [[species|species]] found nowhere else, including Nilgiri tahrs, purple frogs and many orchids. The lion-tailed macaque is one of their best-known residents.

Saving it means saving its forest, which also protects water supplies for millions of people in southern India. Rope bridges for monkeys may sound new, but people in Meghalaya have been growing bridges across rivers for centuries, as you can see with the [[@india-wonder-living-root-bridges|living root bridges]].

text: A dam is a giant wall across a river. Water piles up behind it into a deep lake called a [[reservoir|reservoir]]. Near the bottom of the dam, big pipes called penstocks let water rush downhill. At the end of each pipe the water slams into a [[turbine|turbine]], a wheel with curved blades, and spins it round very fast.

The turbine is joined by a shaft to a [[generator|generator]], where [[@magnets-how|magnets]] spin past coils of wire and make electricity. The water then flows out at the bottom and carries on down the river. The higher the water falls and the more of it there is, the more power comes out.

Where does the energy really come from? The Sun. Its heat lifts water from the sea as vapour, which falls as rain and snow on high mountains. A hydropower station collects that water on its way back down, as part of the [[@water-cycle|water cycle]].

st.prompt: Two power stations have the same amount of water flowing through them each second. Which one makes more electricity?

options.t: The one where the water falls from higher up
The one with the wider river
They make exactly the same

st.reveal: Water falling from higher up is moving faster by the time it hits the turbine, so it carries more energy. Engineers call the height of the drop the "head". More head and more water both mean more power.

myth: A hydroelectric dam uses up the river's water to make electricity.
The water flows through the turbines and carries on down the river. What a dam does change is when and how the water flows, and some is lost by evaporation from the lake behind it.

sec.t:
[[@hoover-dam|The Hoover Dam]] on the Colorado River, on the border between Nevada and Arizona, was finished in 1936. It is 221 metres tall, taller than a 60-storey building, and the lake behind it, Lake Mead, became one of the largest reservoirs in the USA. Thousands of workers built it during the Great Depression, when jobs were scarce.

In India, the Bhakra Dam on the Sutlej River, finished in 1963, stands about 226 metres tall. Its water and electricity helped turn Punjab and Haryana into major wheat-growing states. Prime Minister [[@nehru|Jawaharlal Nehru]] famously called projects like this "the temples of modern India". Today, India's tallest dam is the Tehri Dam in [[@uttarakhand|Uttarakhand]], at about 260 metres.

Some hydropower stations work like giant [[@batteries|batteries]]. They have two reservoirs, one high and one low. When there is spare electricity, often from sunny or windy afternoons, pumps push water up to the top lake. When people need extra power, the water is let back down through the turbines.

This is called pumped storage. India and the USA are both building more of it, to back up solar and wind power when the Sun sets or the wind drops.

Big dams bring electricity, drinking water, [[irrigation|irrigation]] and protection from [[@floods-why|floods]]. They can also flood villages, farmland and forests, forcing many families to move. They block fish from swimming upstream and trap the silt that rivers carry to their deltas.

In India, the Sardar Sarovar Dam on [[@narmada|the Narmada River]] was opposed for decades by the Narmada Bachao Andolan, a movement led by people who would lose their homes. Supporters said the dam would bring water to drought-hit regions of Gujarat and Rajasthan. It was completed in 2017. The debate over how to balance these gains and losses continues wherever new dams are planned.

text: A clay pot, such as a matka or a surahi, is full of tiny holes, too small to see. When you fill it with water, a little seeps slowly through the walls to the outside surface. There it [[evaporation|evaporates]], turning from liquid into invisible water vapour.

Evaporation needs energy. The water takes that energy as heat from whatever it's touching, which is the pot. So as water evaporates from the outside, the pot loses heat, and so does the water inside. The water can end up several degrees cooler than the air around it.
It's the same reason a wet T-shirt feels cold in a breeze, and why your body [[@sweat|sweats]] on a hot day.

Clay isn't cold on its own. A dry clay pot warms up like anything else. The cooling comes from water seeping through tiny holes in the clay and evaporating from the outside, carrying heat away.

sec.t:
Evaporation happens fastest when the air is dry and moving. Dry air has plenty of room for more water vapour, so water escapes into it quickly. A breeze carries the damp air away and brings fresh, dry air.

That's why a matka works brilliantly in the dry heat of a Rajasthan summer and much less well in humid Kolkata or Mumbai during the [[@monsoon|monsoon]]. When the air is already full of moisture, evaporation slows down, and so does the cooling. People in many places keep their pots in a shady, airy corner, sometimes on a stand with a wet cloth around the base.

In northern Nigeria in the 1990s, a teacher named Mohammed Bah Abba popularised a simple cooler. Put one clay pot inside a bigger one, fill the gap between them with wet sand, and cover the top with a damp cloth. As water evaporates from the sand and the outer pot, the inner pot stays cool.

Farmers used these pot-in-pot coolers to keep tomatoes, peppers and other vegetables fresh for days or weeks longer, instead of hurrying to sell them before they spoiled. He won an international award for the idea in 2000. Similar coolers, often called zeer pots, are used in dry regions of Africa and Asia.

The same trick cools whole rooms. In north India, many homes use a "desert cooler", a box with a fan behind pads of wet straw or wood shavings. Hot, dry air is pulled through the wet pads, and the evaporating water cools it before it blows into the room. In older times, people hung mats of fragrant *khus* grass in doorways and splashed them with water.

In the dry south-western USA, in states like [[@grand-canyon-state|Arizona]], people use almost identical machines called swamp coolers. They use far less electricity than an [[@air-conditioning|air conditioner]], but like the matka, they only work well when the air is dry. In a humid [[climate|climate]], they mostly make the room damp.

text: Musical instruments are grouped by what vibrates to make the sound. Every sound is a shaking of the air, and something has to start that shaking. It might be a string, a tight skin, a column of air inside a tube, or the solid body of the instrument itself.

So a [[@sitar-strings|sitar]] and a violin sit together, because both have strings. A [[@tabla|tabla]] and a snare drum sit together, because both have a stretched skin. The same idea was written down in India about 2,000 years ago, and museums around the world still use a version of it today.

myth: Brass instruments are the ones made of brass, and woodwinds are the ones made of wood.
The groups depend on how the sound starts. Many flutes and saxophones are metal but count as woodwinds. Brass instruments are defined by the player buzzing their lips into a cup-shaped mouthpiece.

sec.t:
The *Natya Shastra*, an old [[@sanskrit|Sanskrit]] book on drama and music, puts instruments into four groups. *Tata* means stretched: instruments with strings, like the [[@veena|veena]]. *Sushira* means hollow: instruments you blow into, like the [[@flutes|bansuri flute]]. *Avanaddha* means covered: drums, where a skin is stretched over a frame or pot. *Ghana* means solid: things you strike that ring by themselves, like cymbals, bells and the clay ghatam pot.

Nobody knows exactly when the book was written. Scholars usually place it somewhere between about 200 BCE and 200 CE. What is clear is that the four groups were sensible enough to last. Teachers of Indian classical music still use the words today, and a student learning the mridangam will be told it is an avanaddha vadya, a covered instrument.

An [[@orchestra|orchestra]] uses four everyday families instead. Strings include violins and cellos. Woodwinds include flutes, clarinets and oboes. Brass includes trumpets and tubas, where the player buzzes their lips. Percussion is everything struck or shaken, from timpani drums to the triangle. In a big symphony orchestra, the string players usually make up more than half of the people on stage.

These families are practical. They tell a conductor which players sit together and which sounds blend well. But they can be a little untidy. A flute is usually metal, yet it counts as a woodwind. A tuba and a trumpet sound very different, yet they share a family because both depend on buzzing lips.

Some instruments refuse to fit neatly. A piano has strings, but hammers hit them, so orchestras often place it with percussion or in a group of its own called keyboards. The [[@harmonium|harmonium]] has a keyboard too, yet its sound comes from small metal reeds shaken by air.

The ghatam is a clay pot, but players also press its mouth against their stomach to change the sound of the air inside. Your own voice is an aerophone of sorts: air from your [[@lungs-breathe|lungs]] shakes two folds in your throat. Sorting instruments turns out to be a bit like sorting animals. The rules work well, and the oddballs are often the most interesting part.

text: Airports check bags and passengers to stop anything dangerous getting onto a plane. A plane is a sealed metal tube flying kilometres above the ground, full of people and fuel. A weapon or a small fire on board is far harder to deal with there than on a train or a bus.

So before you board, your bags go through an X-ray machine and you walk through a [[@metal-detectors|metal detector]] or [[@how-metal-detector-airport|body scanner]]. Officers look for weapons, explosives and things that could start a fire, like some batteries, lighters and fuel. Most of the time they find nothing worrying, just too much toothpaste. It is one of the last steps in the long chain that makes an [[@airports|airport]] work.

st.reveal: Lithium batteries can overheat and burn if damaged. In the cabin, the crew will spot the smoke at once and have extinguishers and special bags ready. In the hold, a fire could spread before anyone noticed.

The X-ray dose in a bag scanner is tiny and does no harm to electronics, food or medicines. The only thing that can sometimes be affected is old-style camera film, which is why some photographers ask for it to be checked by hand.

sec.t:
In the 1960s and early 1970s, there were many hijackings, when people took over planes by force. Passengers were rarely searched. In 1973 the USA began screening every airline passenger with metal detectors and bag X-rays.

After the attacks of 11 September 2001, when hijacked planes were flown into buildings in New York and near Washington, checks became much stricter. The USA set up the Transportation Security Administration, the TSA, that November. In India, airport security is overseen by the Bureau of Civil Aviation Security, and since 2000 the Central Industrial Security Force has guarded most big airports.

An X-ray scanner shines a beam through your bag. Dense things block more X-rays than light ones. The computer colours the picture: orange for things made from plants and animals, like food, leather or clothes, green for some plastics, and blue for metal. An officer watches a screen and stops the belt if a shape looks odd. Checked suitcases go through their own scanners, out of sight, on conveyor belts beneath the terminal.

{{story:x-rays}}

Many airports now use CT scanners, which take hundreds of pictures from different angles and build a 3D image. Officers can spin it round on screen. At some of these airports, you can leave your laptop and liquids inside your bag.

Body scanners use harmless radio waves to find hidden objects under clothes. They show a cartoon outline of a person, not a real picture. Officers may also wipe a small cloth over a bag or your hands and test it in a machine that can detect tiny traces of explosives.

In 2006, police in Britain stopped a plot to blow up planes with liquid explosives hidden in drink bottles. Since then, many countries have limited liquids in cabin bags to containers of 100 ml or less. Some airports with newer scanners have begun to relax the rule.

Other rules have less to do with attackers and more with fire. Power banks must travel in your cabin bag, where the crew can reach them. In India, dry coconut and some kinds of matches are banned from checked bags because they can catch fire.

Airports keep trying to move people faster. Indian airports introduced DigiYatra in December 2022, letting travellers who sign up walk through gates that use [[@face-recognition|face recognition]] instead of an ID card. Some people welcome the speed. Others worry about [[@privacy|privacy]] and who stores the pictures.

In 2025 the TSA stopped asking most passengers to take off their shoes, a rule it had kept since 2006. On 30 November 2025, the Sunday after Thanksgiving, it screened about 3.13 million people in one day, a record. Trained dogs still patrol many terminals too. A trained sniffer dog can pick out the smell of explosives on a suitcase as it rolls past.

text: India has made wonderful films for children in Hindi, Bengali, Tamil, Malayalam, Marathi and many other languages. Some are fantasies full of magic. Others are gentle, funny stories about ordinary children at school, at home or in the street.

A few favourites that many families love are Satyajit Ray's *Goopy Gyne Bagha Byne* (1969), *Mr. India* (1987), *Makdee* (2002), *The Blue Umbrella* (2005), *Taare Zameen Par* (2007), *Stanley Ka Dabba* (2011), *Chillar Party* (2011) and the Tamil film *Kaakkaa Muttai* (2014). Each shows children as clever, brave and worth listening to.

The ability to fly

st.reveal: Goopy the singer and Bagha the drummer are granted three boons, including music that stops people in their tracks. They use it to prevent a war between two kingdoms, without anyone getting hurt.

India has a long tradition of live-action films made for and about children, in many languages, from Satyajit Ray's fantasies in Bengali to Tamil and Marathi films that have won national awards.

sec.t:
[[@satyajit-ray|Satyajit Ray]] is best known for serious films, but he also made one of India's most loved children's movies. *Goopy Gyne Bagha Byne* follows two hopeless musicians, a singer and a drummer, who are chased out of their villages for making terrible noise. A king of ghosts gives them magic powers, including music that freezes anyone who hears it. They use it to stop a war.

Ray was also a writer for children, and his grandfather Upendrakishore Ray Chowdhury had written the original Goopy and Bagha story. The film's songs are still sung by children in Bengal.

Some of the best Indian children's films are about everyday life. In *Taare Zameen Par*, eight-year-old Ishaan struggles in school until an art teacher realises that he has dyslexia, a difference in the way the brain handles reading, and helps him shine. Many parents said it changed how they thought about children who find school hard.

*Stanley Ka Dabba* is about a boy who never brings lunch to school and a greedy teacher who keeps stealing other children's food. *Chillar Party* follows a gang of children in a Mumbai housing colony who fight to save a stray dog. *I Am Kalam* (2011) tells of a poor boy in Rajasthan who is inspired by [[@apj-kalam|A.P.J. Abdul Kalam]] and dreams of going to school.

In *Kaakkaa Muttai*, two brothers from a Chennai slum see a new pizza shop and become determined to taste a pizza, though it costs more than their family can spare. The film is funny and sharp, and it won the National Film Award for Best Children's Film. Like many films from [[@cinema-south|South India]], it reached viewers across the country through subtitles.

In 1955, the Government of India set up the Children's Film Society, India, to make and show films for young audiences. It produced hundreds of films and ran the International Children's Film Festival, where the top prize is the Golden Elephant. The festival was held in Hyderabad for many years, and children sat on its juries to help pick the winners. In the early 2020s, the society was merged into the National Film Development Corporation, which continues some of its work. Today, streaming services also commission Indian films and series for children, giving new storytellers a chance.

text: Durga Puja is a Hindu festival that honours the goddess Durga. In Hindu tradition, she defeated Mahishasura, a buffalo demon whom none of the gods could beat alone. It is celebrated across India, but nowhere quite as grandly as in Kolkata and the rest of West Bengal.

For five main days in September or October, Kolkata fills with pandals, temporary structures built to house clay images of Durga and her children. Some neighbourhoods spend months planning theirs. Millions of people walk from one pandal to the next late into the night, eating [[@street-food|street food]] and admiring the art.

options.t: Switch on the radio to hear the same recorded programme

st.reveal: All India Radio broadcasts Mahishasura Mardini, a programme of chants, songs and storytelling. The famous narration by Birendra Krishna Bhadra was recorded decades ago and is still played every year, and many families listen together in the dark.

d.try: Design your own theme pandal on paper. Choose a theme, such as the ocean, a rainforest or a space station, and draw the outside, the entrance and where the goddess would stand inside. Use only everyday materials in your plan, such as bamboo, cloth, paper and clay, as real pandal makers often do.
myth: Durga Puja and Navratri are completely different festivals.

Both honour the goddess at the same time of year. In Bengal and eastern India, the celebration centres on Durga Puja and her victory over Mahishasura; elsewhere it may be celebrated as Navratri and Dussehra, with different customs.
facts: September or October, in the month of Ashwin
Shashthi to Dashami (sixth to tenth day)

sec.t:
Durga is shown with ten arms, each holding a weapon given by a different god, and riding a lion. At her feet lies Mahishasura. Beside her stand her four children: Lakshmi, goddess of wealth; Saraswati, goddess of learning; Ganesh, remover of obstacles; and Kartik, the warrior.

In Bengal, Durga's arrival is also seen as a daughter coming home. Many people believe she visits her parents' house each autumn with her children, then returns to her husband, Shiva, in the Himalayas. So the festival feels like a family reunion, happy and a little sad at the end.

In the 1700s and 1800s, rich families in Calcutta held grand Durga Pujas in their mansions, inviting guests and British officials. One of the best known, at Shobhabazar Rajbari, dates back to 1757.

In the early 1900s, neighbourhood committees began holding sarbojanin pujas, meaning "for everyone". Anyone could visit, whatever their caste or income. These community pujas spread across the city and became the heart of the festival. Today [[@kolkata|Kolkata]] has thousands of them.

Since the 1990s, many committees have competed to build theme pandals. One year a pandal might copy a famous temple, the next it might be made of clay cups, buttons or bicycle parts. Some show scenes from village life; others take on subjects like [[@climate-change|climate change]] or the Chandrayaan mission to the Moon.

Companies give prizes for the best pandals, images and lighting. Artists, many from small towns and villages, travel to the city for months of work. This is one reason UNESCO described the festival as a public art event as well as a religious one.

On Dashami, the last day, married women smear red sindoor on the goddess and on each other, a custom called sindoor khela. Then the images are carried through the streets, with drums called dhak, to be immersed in the river.

Because paints and decorations can pollute water, Kolkata now cleans the river quickly after immersion, and many groups use natural colours. The festival ends with people visiting elders and saying "Shubho Bijoya". Many begin counting the days until next year's Puja almost at once, a feeling shared by fans of [[@ganesh-chaturthi|Ganesh Chaturthi]] in Mumbai.

text: Sachin Tendulkar is called the Little Master because he was short, about 1.65 metres (5 feet 5 inches), and because he mastered batting like almost nobody before him. The nickname had been used earlier for another great Mumbai batter, Sunil Gavaskar, and passed to Sachin as he broke Gavaskar's records.
He played international cricket for 24 years, from 1989 to 2013. He scored more runs in Tests and one-day internationals than anyone else, and is the only player with 100 international centuries.

myth: Sachin was a natural genius who never needed to practise much.
He was famous for practising for hours, even late in his career. He often prepared for particular bowlers by practising on special pitches to copy the conditions he would face.

sec.t:
Sachin grew up in Bandra, in [[@mumbai|Mumbai]]. He was a mischievous child, and his elder brother Ajit took him to Ramakant Achrekar, a coach who trained boys at Shivaji Park. Sachin practised for hours every day, often playing several matches across the city in a single afternoon, travelling between them on his coach's scooter.

In 1988, aged 14, he and his friend Vinod Kambli put on 664 runs together in a school match, a partnership that was then a world record at any level.

Over his career Sachin scored 15,921 [[@test-cricket|Test]] runs and 18,426 one-day runs, both [[@world-records|world records]]. He hit 51 Test centuries and 49 one-day centuries. In 2010, against South Africa in Gwalior, he became the first man to score 200 in a one-day international.

He played 200 Test matches, more than anyone else. His Test batting [[@averages|average]] was 53.78, which means he scored that many runs on average every time he was out. His batting was neat and balanced, using a heavy [[@cricket-bat|bat]] of about 1.5 kg, heavier than most players used. He was a handy bowler too, sending down leg-spin, off-spin and medium pace, and took more than 200 international wickets.

Sachin played in six World Cups, from 1992 to 2011. In 2003 he was player of the [[tournament|tournament]], but India lost the final to Australia.

In 2011 India won at last, in his home city. After the final at the Wankhede Stadium, his teammates carried him on their shoulders. [[@virat-kohli|Virat Kohli]], then 22, said Sachin had carried the burden of the nation for 21 years, so it was their turn to carry him.

For Indian fans in the 1990s, India often seemed to depend on Sachin alone. Many people say they switched off the TV when he got out. He batted in an age of great fast bowlers, before helmets were as safe as today, relying on quick [[@reflexes|reflexes]] and footwork.

He retired after his 200th Test, at the Wankhede in November 2013. That same day the government announced he would receive the Bharat Ratna, India's highest civilian award. He was 40, its youngest recipient, and the first sportsperson to receive it. He later served six years as a member of the Rajya Sabha, [[@parliament-india|Parliament]]'s upper house.

text: For most of the 1980s, India had one TV channel: Doordarshan, run by the government. Because there was nothing else on, the whole country watched the same shows at the same time. Families, neighbours and sometimes whole villages gathered around a single set.

The biggest of all were two serials based on the great epics. Ramanand Sagar's *Ramayan* (1987–88) and B. R. Chopra's *Mahabharat* (1988–90) emptied streets every Sunday morning. Around them were dozens of other favourites, from *[[@malgudi|Malgudi Days]]* to the weekly film song show *Chitrahaar*.

A quiz for viewers to post answers to

st.reveal: The veteran actor Ashok Kumar appeared at the end of each episode to talk about what had happened. The show was designed to raise issues such as family size and girls' education, and viewers sent in huge numbers of letters.

myth: In the Doordarshan years, Indian TV was only news and lectures.

Doordarshan did show plenty of news and educational programmes, but it also had comedies, cartoons, science shows, detective serials and the Sunday film. Many of those shows are still remembered fondly.

sec.t:
In the early 1980s, a TV set was expensive, and many homes did not have one. Those who did often found their living room full of guests at showtime. Children sat on the floor, and neighbours brought snacks.

The 1982 Asian Games in Delhi brought colour TV to India, and Doordarshan quickly built more transmitters. By the end of the decade, most Indians lived within reach of a signal. Satellites, as [[@satellites-india|India's satellites]] explains, carried the pictures from Delhi to the rest of the country.

When *Ramayan* began in January 1987, nobody expected what followed. On Sunday mornings, shops shut, weddings were timed around it, and roads emptied. Some viewers garlanded their TV sets and lit incense in front of them. The actors who played Rama and Sita were greeted like gods in public.

*Mahabharat* followed in 1988, with 94 episodes. Its theme song and the narrator's line "Main samay hoon" (I am Time) are still recognised by millions. Both stories come from ancient texts, the [[@ramayana|Ramayana]] and the Mahabharata.

Not everything was serious. *Malgudi Days* (1986) brought [[@rk-narayan|R. K. Narayan's]] stories of a small South Indian town to the screen, with sketches by his brother, the cartoonist R. K. Laxman. Its [[@behind-theme-music|whistled theme tune]] is famous. Children sang along to the Hindi version of the Japanese cartoon *[[@jungle-book|The Jungle Book]]*, with its song "Jungle jungle baat chali hai".

*Turning Point* explained science in Hindi and English, and *Surabhi* showed Indian culture and crafts, with viewers sending in millions of postcards for its quiz. *Krishi Darshan*, a programme for farmers, has run since 1967.

In the early 1990s, satellite dishes and cable wires brought private channels into Indian homes. Suddenly there were dozens of channels, then hundreds. Families no longer watched the same thing at the same time.

Then, in March 2020, offices and schools closed during the COVID-19 lockdown. Doordarshan brought back *Ramayan* and *Mahabharat*, and grandparents, parents and children watched together once more. For a few weeks, it felt a little like Sunday mornings in 1987.

text: Your body works best at about 37 °C on the inside, and it has clever ways of [[@body-temperature|keeping that temperature steady]]. When you get cold, it fights to protect that temperature. First, blood vessels in your skin narrow so that less heat escapes. Then your muscles start shivering to make extra heat. You may also get goosebumps and feel the urge to curl up.
If you stay cold for too long, those defences can't keep up. Your inside temperature starts to drop. Below 35 °C, doctors call it hypothermia, and it is a medical emergency.

st.prompt: On a freezing day, why do your fingers and toes get cold before the rest of you?

options.t: Your body sends less blood to them to keep your middle warm
Fingers and toes have no blood vessels
Cold air can only touch the ends of your body

st.reveal: When you are cold, tiny blood vessels near the skin narrow, especially in your hands and feet. Less warm blood reaches them, so they cool down, but more heat stays around your heart, lungs and brain, where you need it most.

d.try: Hold an ice cube in a napkin against the back of your hand for 30 seconds, then look at the skin. It will probably look paler, because the blood vessels there have narrowed. Watch how long it takes for the normal colour to come back as the skin warms up.
myth: You lose most of your body heat through your head.
Your head loses heat at about the same rate as any other uncovered part of your body. A hat helps because your head is often the only part left uncovered, not because it is special.

muscles tighten and relax rapidly to make heat

sec.t:
Your brain has a built-in thermostat, part of a region called the hypothalamus. When [[sensor|sensors]] in your skin report cold, it sends out orders. The first is to squeeze the small blood vessels near your skin.

This is why cold hands look pale or even bluish. Your body is choosing to keep warm blood around your heart, lungs and brain and let your fingers, toes, nose and ears cool down. It is a smart trade, but it is also why those parts are the first to get numb, clumsy and, in very harsh cold, frostbitten.

If narrowing the blood vessels isn't enough, your muscles start to shiver. They tighten and relax many times a second. All that work produces heat, and strong shivering can raise heat production several times above normal. It also burns through energy fast, which is one reason people get very hungry in the cold.

[[@goosebumps|Goosebumps]] come from tiny muscles that pull each hair upright. In furry animals, raised hair traps a thicker layer of warm air. Humans have too little body hair for that to help much, so goosebumps are a leftover from our hairy ancestors.

Babies have a special tissue called brown fat that burns energy to make heat without shivering. Adults keep a little of it, mostly around the neck and shoulders.

{{story:penguins-cold}}

Mild hypothermia makes people shiver hard, feel tired and fumble with simple things. As the body cools further, shivering may actually stop, speech becomes slurred and the person gets confused. That is why mountaineers and soldiers are trained to watch each other for these signs.

Frostbite happens when skin and the flesh beneath it freeze. Ice crystals form inside the tissue and damage it. Indian Army soldiers on the Siachen Glacier, where winter temperatures can drop below −40 °C, wear special boots, gloves and face masks to avoid it. In places like Alaska and Minnesota, schools sometimes close on days when the wind chill is dangerously low.

If someone seems badly chilled, the right thing to do is get them somewhere warm and dry and tell an adult straight away, so that help can be called.

sec.h: Why wind and wet make it worse
sec.t:
Still air is a good [[insulator|insulator]]. Wind blows away the thin layer of warm air next to your skin and replaces it with cold air, which is why a windy day feels colder than the thermometer says. Weather forecasters call this "wind chill".

Water is even worse. It pulls heat out of the body about 25 times faster than air at the same temperature. Wet clothes or a fall into icy water can chill someone very quickly.

Layers work better than one thick coat, because each layer traps air. A thin inner layer keeps sweat off your skin, a fluffy middle layer holds warm air, and an outer layer stops wind and rain. People in [[@ladakh|Ladakh]] and other cold places have known this for centuries, wearing thick woollen robes and felt boots. Warm drinks and regular meals help too, because your body needs fuel to keep its fire burning.

text: When you look at a phone with face recognition, it takes a picture of your face. It turns that picture into a set of numbers that describe its shape, such as the distances between your eyes, nose, mouth and chin. It compares those numbers with the ones it saved when you set it up. If they match closely enough, the phone opens.

The best systems use infrared light, which our eyes can't see, to measure your face in 3D. A type of [[@ai-what|artificial intelligence]] does the matching, and it keeps learning small changes, like a new haircut or glasses.

st.prompt: Some cheaper phones recognise faces using only the normal front camera. What is their biggest weakness?

options.t: They can sometimes be fooled by a photo of the owner
They only work in the dark
They can't tell a face from a hand

st.reveal: A flat camera sees only a flat image, so a good photo or video might trick it. Phones that measure depth with infrared light check the real 3D shape of a face, which a printed photo does not have.

d.try: Look at photos of family members and try to describe what makes each face recognisable using only measurements, such as "eyes far apart" or "long chin". Swap descriptions with a friend and see if they can match each description to the right photo. That's roughly what early face recognition programs tried.
myth: Face recognition works equally well on everyone.

A large 2019 study by the US standards agency NIST found that many systems made more mistakes with some groups, depending on age, sex and skin colour. The best systems have improved, but accuracy still depends on how they were trained and used.

sec.t:
Apple's Face ID, launched in 2017, has a tiny projector that sprays more than 30,000 invisible [[infrared|infrared]] dots onto your face. An infrared camera photographs the pattern. Where your nose sticks out, the dots bunch differently than on your cheeks. From that, the phone builds a depth map, a 3D model of your face.

Because it uses its own invisible light, it works in a dark room. And because it checks depth, a flat photo won't fool it. Many systems also check that your eyes are open and looking at the screen, so nobody can open your phone while you sleep.

Apple says Face ID has about a one-in-a-million chance of opening for a random person. But for [[@twins|identical twins]], close siblings and children under 13, whose faces are still changing, the odds of a mix-up are higher. For those people, a passcode is safer.

Cheaper phones often use only the ordinary front camera. They are handy but easier to fool, which is why banking apps on such phones may still ask for a fingerprint or PIN.

Face recognition is now used at airports, offices and stadiums. In India, [[@airport-security|the DigiYatra system]], launched at Delhi, Bengaluru and Varanasi airports in December 2022, lets passengers walk through gates by showing their face instead of a boarding pass. US airports use face checks for some international travellers.

The idea goes back to the 1960s, when the American researcher Woody Bledsoe and his team measured features on photos by hand, then had a computer compare them.

Police in some places use face recognition to search crowds or check photos of suspects. Supporters say it helps find missing children and criminals. Critics worry about mass tracking of ordinary people and wrong matches. In the USA, several people have been wrongly arrested after a face match, and some cities, including [[@san-francisco|San Francisco]] in 2019, banned their police from using it.

A 2019 study by NIST found that many systems made more mistakes with some groups of people than others. Countries are still deciding what rules should protect [[@privacy|privacy]] while allowing useful uses.

text: A container ship is a floating warehouse built around one idea: put everything in identical steel boxes. Shoes, phones, bananas and car parts all travel in containers of the same standard sizes. Cranes can lift any of them, trucks and trains can carry any of them, and ships can stack them like building blocks.

The biggest ships today are about 400 metres long and 61 metres wide. They can carry more than 24,000 TEU, the unit for one twenty-foot container. Stacked below and above deck, the boxes tower higher than a ten-storey building.
A single giant diesel engine turns one enormous [[propeller|propeller]]. The ship crosses oceans at around 30 to 40 km an hour, with a crew small enough to fit in a school classroom.

sec.t:
Before containers, cargo was loaded piece by piece: sacks, crates and barrels carried by dock workers. Loading a ship could take a week, and goods were often lost or stolen.

In 1956, an American trucking businessman named Malcom McLean had a better idea. He fitted an old tanker, the *Ideal X*, to carry 58 truck trailer boxes from New Jersey to Texas. Loading took hours, not days.

Containers soon became standard sizes. Today, cranes at a big port can move a container every minute or two. Every box has its own ID code, so computers can track it from factory to shop. Containers made moving goods across oceans so cheap that they changed where things are made. A shirt can be sewn in Bangladesh and sold in Texas a few weeks later.

A steel ship floats because its hull [[@floating-ships|pushes aside]] a huge weight of water, much more than the steel itself. [[ballast|Ballast]] tanks inside fill with seawater or empty out to keep the ship level as boxes are loaded and unloaded.

At the front, just under the water, many big ships have a rounded bulb. This bulbous bow makes its own small wave that cancels part of the ship's main bow wave, so the ship slides through the water using less fuel.

Stopping is the slow part. A fully loaded giant can take several kilometres to come to a halt, so captains plan turns and stops long in advance. Near ports, tugboats help push and pull. A local pilot, who knows every sandbank, usually comes aboard to guide the ship in.

{{story:floating-ships}}

sec.h: When one ship blocked the world
sec.t:
In March 2021, the 400-metre *Ever Given* turned sideways in a sandstorm and got stuck across the [[@suez-canal|Suez Canal]]. For six days, hundreds of ships queued at both ends. Diggers, dredgers and tugs finally worked it free at a high tide.

The jam showed how much the world depends on these ships. Experts at the United Nations estimate that around 80% of world trade by volume travels by sea.

India's big container ports include JNPA near Mumbai and Mundra in Gujarat. In June 2025, the *MSC Irina*, one of the largest container ships ever built, docked at the new Vizhinjam port near Thiruvananthapuram in [[@kerala|Kerala]]. Vizhinjam has deep water close to shore, so giant ships can berth there without long channels being dug.

Container ships burn a lot of fuel, mostly heavy oil, and shipping produces about 3% of the world's [[greenhouse-gas|greenhouse gases]]. To cut that, some new ships run on liquefied gas or methanol. Engineers are testing giant sails and kites, and many ships already practise "slow steaming", sailing slower to save fuel. Even a few knots make a big difference when your ship weighs as much as a small mountain of steel.

text: The Cholas were a Tamil [[dynasty|dynasty]] who ruled from the [[fertile|fertile]] Kaveri delta in Tamil Nadu. They were most powerful from about 850 to 1279 CE.

Rich from rice farming and trade, the Cholas built a strong army and a navy. Under Rajaraja I and his son Rajendra I, they conquered much of south India and northern Sri Lanka, and took over the [[@maldives|Maldives]]. In 1025 they [[@chola-navy|sent a fleet]] across the Bay of Bengal to attack the Srivijaya kingdom in Malaysia and Sumatra. Their aim was largely to control the busy sea trade between India, Southeast Asia and China. At home they built huge [[granite|granite]] temples and cast some of the finest bronze [[sculpture|sculptures]] ever made.

myth: Ancient Indian kings never went to sea, and only traded by land.
South Indian kingdoms, especially the Cholas, had strong links across the ocean. Chola ships carried armies to Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia, and Chola envoys travelled to China.

sec.t:
The Kaveri river spreads into many channels as it nears the sea, watering a wide green delta. Early Chola kings learned to manage that water.

The Kallanai, a stone dam across the Kaveri, is traditionally linked to Karikala, a Chola king who lived around 2,000 years ago. Rebuilt and strengthened over time, it still guides water into canals today, making it one of the oldest water works in the world still in use. Reliable harvests fed large populations, and taxes on rice paid for armies and temples.

Rajendra I, who ruled from 1014 to 1044, pushed further. His army marched north to the Ganga, and he built a new capital called Gangaikonda Cholapuram, "city of the one who took the Ganga".

Then, in 1025, he sent a fleet against Srivijaya, a rich sea kingdom that controlled the Strait of Malacca, the narrow passage between Malaysia and Sumatra. Chola inscriptions list the ports that were captured, including Kadaram, today's Kedah in Malaysia. Sailors timed voyages with the [[@monsoon|monsoon]] winds. The Cholas did not rule Southeast Asia for long, but the raid made sure Tamil merchants could trade freely.

The Cholas left thousands of inscriptions in [[@tamil-ancient|Tamil]]. The most famous for ordinary life are at Uttaramerur, near Kanchipuram, from around 920 CE.

They describe how the village chose its council. Names of qualified men were written on palm-leaf tickets and placed in a pot. A young boy then drew them out. The rules even barred people who had been dishonest, or whose relatives had been, from standing. This system of choosing by lot is different from modern [[@vote-how|voting]], but it shows a village running its own affairs a thousand years ago.

Chola artists made bronze images of gods using the lost-wax method. They modelled a figure in beeswax, covered it in clay, melted the wax out and poured metal into the hollow.

The most famous image is Shiva as Nataraja, the lord of dance, dancing inside a ring of flames. Chola bronzes are carried in temple processions to this day, and museums from [[@chennai|Chennai]] to New York treasure them. A statue of Nataraja stands outside [[@extreme-biggest-machines|CERN]], the physics laboratory in [[@switzerland|Switzerland]], a gift from India in 2004.

text: Kochi, on the coast of [[@kerala|Kerala]], has been a trading port for over 600 years. Its harbour sits where backwater [[lagoon|lagoons]] meet the Arabian Sea, and its hinterland grows [[@food-pepper-black-gold|black pepper]], cardamom and other [[@spices|spices]] that the world wanted. Traders came from Arabia, China and, later, Portugal, the Netherlands and Britain.

Many stayed. Jewish, Christian, Muslim, Hindu, Gujarati and Konkani communities built homes, temples, churches, mosques and a famous synagogue side by side. That's why a short walk in old Kochi can take you past buildings from several continents. The city has long been one of India's great meeting places.

st.prompt: Kochi's harbour is one of the best on India's west coast. According to tradition, how was it created?

st.reveal: The story goes that floods on the Periyar river in 1341 opened a channel to the sea at Kochi and silted up the old port of Muziris to the north. Trade moved to Kochi, and the town grew quickly.

n.certNote: Kochi's trading history is well documented. Some popular stories, such as who first brought the Chinese fishing nets and exactly how the 1341 flood created the harbour, are traditions that historians can't fully confirm.

sec.t:
Along the waterfront at Fort Kochi stand the famous Chinese fishing nets, called cheena vala in [[@malayalam|Malayalam]]. Each is a giant wooden frame, up to about 10 m high, with a net hanging from it. A team of fishers lowers it into the water using big stones as counterweights, then hauls it up with the catch.

Many people believe the nets were brought by Chinese traders, perhaps around the time of the admiral [[@zheng-he|Zheng He]], whose fleets visited the Kerala coast in the early 1400s. Others think the Portuguese brought them from their colony at Macau. Nobody knows for certain. Fewer nets work today, because catches near the shore have fallen and repairing the big wooden frames is costly, but the ones still standing are among Kochi's best-known sights.

In 1498, the Portuguese explorer Vasco da Gama reached Kerala by sea. The Portuguese soon set up a fort in Kochi. Da Gama died in Kochi in 1524 and was buried in St Francis Church, one of the oldest European-built churches in India. His remains were later taken back to Portugal, but his first gravestone is still there.

In 1663, [[@dutch-french-india|the Dutch took over]]. They rebuilt the Mattancherry Palace, first built by the Portuguese as a gift for the Raja, so it became known as the Dutch Palace. Its walls carry beautiful [[mural|murals]] from the Ramayana. The British took control in the late 1700s, and Kochi later grew into a major naval base and shipbuilding port. India's first home-built [[@aircraft-carriers|aircraft carrier]], INS Vikrant, was built at Cochin Shipyard.

Jewish traders lived in Kerala for many centuries. In 1568, a community known as the Paradesi Jews built a synagogue in Mattancherry. Its floor is covered with hand-painted blue and white tiles brought from China. Most of Kochi's Jews moved to Israel after 1948, and only a handful remain, but the synagogue is still cared for.

Modern Kochi looks forward as well as back. In 2012, the city launched the Kochi-Muziris Biennale, a big contemporary art festival held in old warehouses. In 2015, its airport became the world's first to run fully on [[@solar-panels|solar power]]. In 2023, it opened a Water Metro, with electric boats linking the islands of its backwaters.

text: Varanasi, also called Kashi and Banaras, sits on the western bank of the Ganga in Uttar Pradesh. [[archaeologist|Archaeologists]] digging at Rajghat, at the city's northern edge, have found signs that people lived there more than 2,500 years ago. Hindu texts describe Kashi as a holy city from very early times.

What makes Varanasi special is that it has never really stopped being lived in. Cities in other places rose and were abandoned, but here people kept praying, trading, studying and [[weaving|weaving]] beside the same river for thousands of years. In 1897 the American writer [[@mark-twain|Mark Twain]] visited and wrote that it was "older than history, older than tradition, older even than legend".

st.reveal: Each evening, priests wave large brass lamps, ring bells and chant in honour of the river Ganga. Crowds watch from the steps and from boats, and many float small leaf bowls with flowers and a lamp on the water.

n.certNote: Archaeologists agree Varanasi is very old, but estimates of its age differ. Digs at Rajghat point to settlement from around the early first millennium BCE, while Hindu tradition sees the city as far older.

It is one of the oldest cities still lived in, but no one can prove it is the very oldest. Places such as Damascus, Jericho and Byblos in West Asia also claim many thousands of years of settlement.

sec.t:
Along the river, Varanasi is lined with ghats, wide stone steps leading down to the water. There are more than 80 of them, stretching for several kilometres. At dawn, people come to bathe, pray, wash clothes, do yoga and sell flowers. Boats row slowly past.

Every evening at Dashashwamedh Ghat, priests perform the Ganga Aarti. They wave large brass lamps in circles, while bells ring and conch shells sound. For many Hindus, the Ganga is a goddess, and bathing in her water at Kashi is very holy.

Hindus believe that Varanasi is the city of Shiva. The Kashi Vishwanath temple is one of the most important Shiva temples in India. The present building was put up in 1780 by Ahilyabai Holkar, a queen of Indore, and its spire was later covered in gold given by Maharaja [[@ranjit-singh|Ranjit Singh]].

Many Hindus believe that dying in Kashi, or being cremated on its ghats, frees the soul from the cycle of rebirth. That is why some elderly people come to spend their last years in the city. At Manikarnika Ghat, cremation fires have burned day and night for centuries.

Varanasi's weavers, many of them Muslim families, make [[@art-banarasi|Banarasi saris]] with patterns in gold and silver thread. A single fine sari can take weeks to [[@weaving-saree|weave]] on a handloom. They are often worn at weddings across India.

The city is also a home of Hindustani classical music. The great [[@shehnai-bismillah|shehnai]] player Ustad Bismillah Khan lived here and played every day by the river. In 1916, Madan Mohan Malaviya founded Banaras Hindu University, now one of the largest residential universities in Asia.

The Ganga at Varanasi is under pressure from sewage and waste from towns upstream. The government and local groups have spent years building treatment plants and cleaning the ghats, with mixed results. People who live here see the river as a mother, and they also want her to be clean.

text: Black pepper grows on a climbing vine native to the rainforests of the Western Ghats in south India. For thousands of years, it was one of the most wanted goods on Earth. Romans, Arabs, Egyptians, Chinese and Europeans paid huge sums for it.

Peppercorns were light, kept for years and could be shipped across oceans without rotting. In places far from India, they could be worth a lot, and they were sometimes used almost like money. That is why pepper earned the nickname "black gold". The hunt for it helped start long sea voyages, wars and [[empire|empires]], including the journey that brought the [[@portuguese-india|Portuguese to India]].

sec.t:
The oldest known pepper found far from India sits in the mummy of Ramesses II, an Egyptian pharaoh who died in 1213 BCE. Scientists examining his body found black peppercorns stuffed into his nostrils, probably as part of the preparation for burial.

Nobody grew pepper in Egypt. Those peppercorns must have travelled from south India, passed from trader to trader, over sea and land. The making of [[@mummies|mummies]] used many precious goods, and pepper was one of them.

In [[medieval|medieval]] Europe, pepper was so valued that people sometimes paid rent, taxes or dowries in peppercorns. In English law, a "peppercorn rent" once meant a real payment in pepper. Today it means a tiny, token rent, because pepper is cheap now.

Venice and Arab traders controlled much of the spice route to Europe and grew rich. Other countries wanted a cut. In 1498, the Portuguese explorer Vasco da Gama sailed around Africa and reached Calicut, now Kozhikode, in Kerala. Soon Portuguese, Dutch, French and British traders were fighting over the spice coast. The British [[@east-india-company|East India Company]] began as a spice trader.

Pepper's bite comes from a chemical called piperine. It tickles heat and pain [[sensor|sensors]] in your mouth, though more gently than the [[capsaicin|capsaicin]] in chillies. Chillies came to India only around the 1500s, from the Americas. Before that, pepper and long pepper were what made Indian food hot.

Black pepper is still the world's most traded spice. Today Vietnam grows the most, and Brazil, Indonesia and India are also big producers. India eats so much of its own pepper that it also [[import|imports]] some.

In Kerala and Karnataka, pepper vines still climb trees in coffee and cardamom gardens, often alongside [[@cardamom-pepper|cardamom]], the other famous spice of the hills. Farmers pick the green berries by hand from ladders, then spread them out to dry on mats. In a few days they turn black and wrinkled, just as they have for thousands of years.

text: Milk boils over because it builds a lid on itself. As milk warms up, [[protein|proteins]] and droplets of fat rise and form a thin skin on top. This skin is the *malai* that some people love and others pick out of their chai.

When the milk underneath gets close to 100°C, steam bubbles start to rise. In plain water, they burst at the surface and the steam escapes. In milk, they get stuck under the skin and inside a froth of proteins. More bubbles pile up below. The foam swells and lifts the skin like a balloon until, in a few seconds, it spills over the edge.

st.reveal: As milk heats, proteins and fat form a thin skin on top. Steam bubbles rising from below get trapped under it and pile up into foam. The foam pushes the skin up until it pours over the rim.

sec.t:
Milk looks simple, but it is a crowded mixture. About 87% is water. The rest is fat, a sugar called [[lactose|lactose]], minerals, and proteins. The two main proteins are casein and whey.

Casein forms tiny clusters that float in the milk. They are so small that they scatter light, which is part of why milk looks white instead of clear. Whey proteins are [[dissolve|dissolved]] in the watery part.

Ordinary bubbles in water pop because the water film around them drains and thins out quickly. Milk proteins coat each bubble and make its wall stronger, the same way soap does in a [[@soap-bubbles-colours|soap bubble]]. So the bubbles last longer and stack up into foam.

Foam takes up far more space than liquid. A thin layer of milk can turn into a tall tower of froth. A steel pot that is only half full can be overflowing within a few seconds.

For thousands of years, boiling was the safest way to kill germs in fresh milk. In the 1860s, the French scientist Louis Pasteur showed that gentle heating could kill many harmful [[microbe|microbes]] in wine. The same idea, called pasteurisation, was later used on milk. Packet milk in India and the USA is usually [[pasteurise|pasteurised]] already, so many families boil it out of habit, or simply because they like it hot.

People have invented lots of ways to stop this. Lower the flame once the milk starts to steam. Use a wider pan, so the skin is thinner and steam escapes. Keep stirring to break the skin.

Some cooks lay a wooden spoon across the pot. It can pop the first bubbles that touch it, but it won't save a pot left on high heat for long. Many Indian kitchens use a metal disc called a milk guard or "milk watcher". It sits at the bottom of the pan and rattles noisily as the milk heats, warning the cook in time.

Sometimes overflowing milk is good news. In Tamil Nadu, people celebrate [[@onam-pongal|Pongal]] by boiling rice and milk in a new pot until it froths over. Everyone shouts "Pongalo Pongal!" as it spills. In many homes across South India, families boil milk over when they move into a new house, as a wish for plenty.

India drinks and cooks with a lot of milk. In 2024–25 it produced about 247 million tonnes, roughly a quarter of the world's total. That number was far smaller in the 1960s, before farmers' [[cooperative|cooperatives]] and the [[@white-revolution|White Revolution]] turned India into a milk giant.
